title: Motor Efficiency Classes IE1 IE2 IE3 IE4: 4 Essential IEC 60034 Facts
text:
Electrical Fundamentals

 Motor Efficiency Classes IE1 IE2 IE3 IE4: 4 Essential IEC 60034 Facts

 Motor efficiency classes are defined by IEC 60034-30-1. This standard sets the minimum efficiency a motor must achieve to belong to a given class.

 IE stands for International Efficiency. The four main classes are IE1, IE2, IE3, and IE4. Each step up means lower energy losses inside the motor.

 This guide explains what each motor efficiency class means and the real efficiency numbers at common power ratings. It also covers which class is mandatory in India and the EU.

 
 IEC 60034-30-1 
 IE1 to IE4 Explained 
 EU Ecodesign Regulation 
 Energy Savings Calculation 
 




 Electric motors consume roughly 45 to 50 percent of all electricity used in industry. Even a 1 percent improvement in motor efficiency translates into thousands of kilowatt-hours saved every year.

 The IE efficiency class on the motor nameplate is the single fastest way to know how much energy a motor wastes before you run it.

 
 
 
 Why Motor Efficiency Classes Were Created


 Before IEC 60034-30 standardised motor efficiency classes, different countries had different efficiency labels. Europe used EFF1, EFF2, EFF3. The USA used NEMA standards.

 Manufacturers had to certify motors differently for every market. This made comparison almost impossible for engineers buying motors internationally.


 The IEC introduced the IE classification in 2008. The 2014 update, IEC 60034-30-1, covers motors from 0.12 kW to 1000 kW at 50 Hz and 60 Hz.

 It gives a single, globally consistent motor efficiency label. IE3 on a nameplate means the same thing whether the motor was made in Germany, India, China, or Brazil.


 Did You Know? The IE classification is not the same as the motor efficiency value itself. IE3 does not mean 93% efficient. It means the motor meets the minimum efficiency threshold set by IEC 60034-30-1 for IE3 at its specific power rating and pole count. A 4-pole 7.5 kW motor must reach at least 90.4% to qualify as IE3 at 50 Hz. A 4-pole 75 kW motor must reach at least 95.0% for IE3 at 50 Hz. The threshold rises with power rating.

Test methods are defined separately in IEC 60034-2-1. This distinction matters: IEC 60034-30-1 defines the class boundaries; IEC 60034-2-1 defines how to measure the efficiency to check against those boundaries.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Motor Efficiency Classes IE1 to IE4: What Each One Means


 
 
 IE1

 Standard Efficiency

 The original baseline class. Now banned from sale in the EU, India, China, and Australia for most motor sizes. Still permitted for special applications like brake motors and explosion-proof motors in some jurisdictions.

 

 
 IE2

 High Efficiency

 Roughly 1 to 2 percentage points above IE1. Now the minimum in many Southeast Asian markets. Permitted in the EU only when the motor is operated with a variable frequency drive (VFD). Equivalent to NEMA Energy Efficient in North America.

 

 
 IE3

 Premium Efficiency

 The current mandatory minimum in the EU, India (from July 2023), China, and Australia for motors above 0.75 kW. Roughly 1 to 2 percentage points above IE2. Equivalent to NEMA Premium Efficiency in North America. The global baseline for new industrial motors.

 

 
 IE4

 Super Premium Efficiency

 Mandatory in the EU from July 2023 for motors from 75 kW to 200 kW. Roughly 1 to 2 percentage points above IE3. At higher power ratings, IE4 often requires synchronous reluctance (SynRM) or permanent magnet (PMSM) motor technology rather than standard cage induction design.

 




 Real Efficiency Numbers: What the IEC 60034-30-1 Table Says


 The efficiency thresholds below are from IEC 60034-30-1:2014 for 4-pole motors at 50 Hz. These are minimum nominal efficiency values. Actual motor efficiency may be higher than the class minimum.


 
 
 Rated Power (kW) IE1 min. efficiency (%) IE2 min. efficiency (%) IE3 min. efficiency (%) IE4 min. efficiency (%) 

 1.5 kW 77.2 82.8 85.3 88.7 

 4 kW 84.2 87.4 89.8 92.3 

 7.5 kW 86.0 88.7 90.4 92.6 

 11 kW 87.6 90.3 91.9 93.6 

 22 kW 89.5 91.6 93.0 94.6 

 37 kW 90.8 92.7 93.9 95.3 

 75 kW 92.7 94.1 95.0 96.1 

 200 kW 94.2 95.4 96.2 97.0 

 375 kW 94.7 95.8 96.5 97.3 

 



 The efficiency gap between IE1 and IE3 is largest at small power ratings (8.1 points at 1.5 kW) and narrows at large ratings (1.8 points at 375 kW).

 Even small percentage-point differences matter more at high power because the absolute energy flowing through the motor is much larger.


 Did You Know? The percentage-point gap between IE classes looks small, but the energy-loss gap is actually much larger. Motor losses are the difference between input power and output power. At 7.5 kW and IE1 efficiency of 86%, the motor loses 1.22 kW as heat. At IE3 efficiency of 90.4%, it loses only 0.79 kW. That is a 35 percent reduction in losses, even though the efficiency only went up by 4.4 percentage points.

This is why engineers who think in percentage-point differences underestimate the real impact of moving from IE1 to IE3. The correct way to compare is to look at loss reduction, not efficiency-point difference.


 How Motor Efficiency Classes Affect Energy Losses


 Motor efficiency is defined as output power divided by input power. The difference is lost as heat. The motor efficiency class determines how low those losses must be.

 The four main loss sources are shown in the tabs below.


 
 
 Copper Losses 
 Iron Losses 
 Friction and Windage 
 Stray Load Losses 
 

 
 Copper Losses (I squared R losses)

 These are caused by current flowing through the resistance of the stator windings and rotor bars. They are proportional to the square of the current and the resistance.

 Higher efficiency motors use more copper in the windings (reducing resistance) and design the rotor with lower-loss materials.
